notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa015c.opp-l: Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'os mnti' for 'os muti', 'rudibili' for 'rugibili', 'csurie nibus' for 'esurientibus', 'crocis' for 'crucis', 'Umlectica' for 'Dialectica'). In ch. II heading, 'Quare expostuletur' rendered as 'Why it is requested'. In line 3, 'a vita Patre' taken as 'from the Father, the Life'. In ch. I, 'hic ab ea ignorabitur' read as 'whoever is ignorant of it here will be ignored by it'; the Latin is compressed.

Line 19: 'de quo Deus' is probably a corruption of 'quod Deus' ('which is God'); translated so. 'cerscendo' read as 'crescendo'. Line 15: 'der est' read as 'Aer est'; psalm references given in Vulgate numbering, corrected from scanning errors (Ps. CIII, CXLV). Line 17: 'probata' read as 'probat'.

Line 21: the text is evidently defective at 'igitur constat quamque animam toto mundo longe ma-gnitudinem corporalis quantitatis intelligat' (words such as 'majorem esse' and the start of a new sentence, probably 'let no one here understand...', are lost); marked [...]. Also defective at 'remeare pos- ditetur', where the end of one sentence and the start of the next (apparently addressing the reader in prayer) are lost; marked [...]. 'concludit' read for 'includit' as printed (sense unchanged). Line 22: 'constitudissima' read as 'constitutos in clarissima'. Line 25: 'et ipsum solum cuncta ex nihilo fecisse probaverit' is printed twice (dittography) and translated once.

Lines 29–30: the scan places 'Quid' at the end of the Disciples' reply; it belongs to the Master's question and is translated there. Line 43: the stray 'prolis, et' is a scanning duplicate from the next line; the word 'mother' is supplied from the chapter heading. Line 40: the text 'de indivi-substantia in pluralitate consistentibus' is garbled; read as 'substantia de individuis in pluralitate consistentibus'. Line 26 contains a duplicated 'individuae per'. Line 50: 'verbum' as 'vere bonum' is a Latin pseudo-etymology. Line 53 heading probably lacks 'Cur'.

Line 58: 'dicitur Filium' — 'Filium' appears stray (perhaps from the next sentence) and is left untranslated. Line 63 is corrupt ('veneratur1. rum'); read as 'veneratur, cum'. Line 64: 'substantialia' read for 'subst nlialin'. Line 65 heading 'Annon aliqui necessaria miseri' read as 'necessario'. Line 66: 'potius' read for 'politis', 'faciam' for 'faciant'. Line 67: 'Dei bonitas' read for 'DA bonitas'. Line 68: 'bona' read for 'bon,'; 'cum ad inconveniens non flectit' read as 'eum ... non flectit'.

Line 70: 'instrumenta in tot substantias produxit' appears defective; a negative such as 'sine' (without) seems lost before 'instrumenta', and is supplied in brackets. Line 74: the text is disordered and corrupt ('Deum quod vivit... Corpora sibi inesse sentunt. Heus quippe vvitaest, et omne quoqne cœlestia'); the words appear displaced, and the translation follows the evident reconstruction (God is life, whatever lives lives by life; the heavenly bodies too perceive...). Line 75: 'sed ut cor est in animali rel pars animalis, ut lucernae lumen...' is awkward; the sense seems to be 'not as the heart is in an animal, but as a lamp's light is in the sun', with 'sed' misplaced.

XXVI: 'malum vel nihil pati' is odd ('suffer evil or nothing'); rendered literally. XXVIII heading ('Whether, had man not sinned...') belongs to the end of XXVII's question. XXIX: 'partim in , nec' has a dropped word, evidently 'cœlo', supplied as [heaven]. XXX: 'nec fuit præteritum, præsens est' seems defective; probably 'nec fuit praeteritum, nec erit futurum, sed praesens est'; the supplement is bracketed. XXXI: 'Angeli animæ' read as 'Angeli [et] animae'.

Line 88: the text reads 'se ipsam videre potest' ('can see itself'); the chapter heading and the sense require a lost 'non', and it is translated so. 'contabulatur' is taken as 'confabulatur' (converses). Line 84: 'convenientia et similitudinis' is read as 'convenientia et similitudo'. Line 96: 'Magistri anima' is taken as 'Magistri animam' (masters [remind] the soul); 'stultius' as 'stultitia' (folly).

Several scanning errors were read as evident: 98 'ci edere' as credere, 'facit bonam' as facit bonum; 100 'sentire credimur' taken as 'credimus', 'scutit' as sentit; 101 'abrtini' as Martini; 104 'non petitos' as non penitus, 'remom' as remoto; 105 'palla' as poena; 107 'admeta' perhaps adempta, and 'quod sit, si' as 'quod si'. In 104 the sentence 'longe res aliter erat quam prius videre non valebant' is awkward and may be corrupt; the sense given is tentative. In 98 'sibi similia' could also mean 'like to it' in the sense of 'akin to the soul'.

113: 'tatium' is evidently corrupt; rendered as 'as reason shows', omitting it. 112: 'scilicet quoque' and 'set sensuale' read as scanning slips. 112: 'non nesciuntur' in the first heaven-figure passage is taken as 'not unknown'. 113: the heading's 'Quid inferri' is obscure, rendered literally. 114: the clause on air and fire is awkwardly constructed ('irrisus computantur'); the rendering gives the probable sense. The '(a)' is a footnote mark and has been left out.

In XLVI 'alta stellarum' read as 'alia stellarum', 'quentum' as 'quantum', and 'hos intem' as 'hos inter' (or similar); in XLVII 'dilicientur/delicientur' read as 'delectentur', 'trabuntur' as 'trahuntur'. 'Lucifer' is taken as the morning star (Venus).

nodes.text: THE KNOWLEDGE OF LIFE, OR ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF TRUE LIFE: ONE BOOK.

CHAPTER ONE. For what purpose rational nature was made. The reason for the work undertaken. Its name. The Wisdom of God, which opened the mouth of the mute (Matt. 9:33), and granted to a braying animal to form human words (Num. 22:28), drives me too, unskilled not only in speech but also in knowledge, to speak, and compels [me] to make known piously to others what is understood through it and about it. By its prompting, therefore, for the benefit, as I hope, of very many, I once again commit myself to be gnawed by the teeth of the envious, and perhaps to be cherished by the hearts of those who love life: since Christ, the truth and the life, says, This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God (John 17:3). It is certainly established that rational nature was made for this alone: that it should understand its maker, the true God, by understanding love [him], and by loving live blessedly and eternally in him who is eternal life. To investigate the essence of the Godhead by reason, then, is to hasten towards eternal life; but to neglect it and remain ignorant of it is surely to hurry towards unending death: for whoever is ignorant of it here will no doubt be ignored by it, when he is at some time separated from the blessed life. Therefore, since very many of the holy Fathers have written many glorious things about this illustrious subject, and have in a way made the matter itself, dense [as it is], more obscure to simpler people, it pleases me to level with my pen, as it were, a kind of path through these thickets, by which weak understandings, leaving the byway of error, may walk freely over the plain of truth. But here perhaps some envious man meets me with a clouded face, and bitterly vomits on me the poison long congealed in his livid heart, saying: Why are you trying to carry wood into the forest, or why do you attempt to drip water into the overflowing sea? Let this rock blunt the biting tooth of so biting a man, and pour the poison he maliciously vomited back into his own entrails, to torment them: Through the envy of the devil death entered the world; those who are on his side imitate him (Wis. 2:24-25). O unhappy envious man, who are tormented by another's happiness and feed upon another's loss, by these very things you prove that you are on his side, since you envy others for knowing what you do not know; and you groan with sick sighs at me because of the pious labour granted me, which you recognise has been denied to you because of sloth, or rather because of envy. Come, wretch, rather vomit up the deadly poison with which you swell, and take the healthful antidote of love. But if not, wasting away with black bile, favour the side of your father. I, however, have no road in common with wasting envy. Entering eagerly the excellent forest of the Scriptures, I will not carry wood into it, as you assert with poisoned tongue, but will try to bring out of it the precious wood of life for those who hunger for righteousness; and I will not delay to draw the sweet draught of life from the sea of Scripture for those who thirst for life. Let all of us faithful, then, run to the tree and fountain of life, by tasting which we may live blessedly for ever. And let the little book receive the name The Knowledge of Life, since in it true life is seen to be made knowable to those slower of understanding.

CHAPTER II. A carnal conception of the heavenly kingdom. How hard it is to set forth the knowledge of God. By what method it is attempted. Why it is requested. The difficulty of the work. DISCIPLES. We give thanks to God, by whose gift we can be clearly assured in doubtful matters. Since, then, you see that we have come together for this very purpose, so that we, travelling towards the homeland, may not grow weary on the road and fail, refresh [us] as you are accustomed with the food and drink of life, and, binding time, which slips away in a course that never returns, with the bonds of questions, make it stable for us: so that its fickleness may not engulf us while idle, but your kindness may raise us, labouring in divine things, to the age that abides for ever.

MASTER. Come eagerly with me to the fruit of the tree of life hanging on the branches of the cross, and with one mind draw from the fountain of life flowing from the Father, the Life, as if from a place of delight, watering paradise, that is, the Church, the garden of delights: if its savour sweetens the palate of your heart, I testify to you that it will at some time satisfy you, who will endure with eternity, from the torrent of its delight.

DISC. Since, savouring carnal things, we cannot think spiritual ones, we picture in our minds the kingdom of heaven as a most bright region, overflowing with every abundance, in which [is] the heavenly Jerusalem, a city richly endowed, famed for merits and riches, and in it God as a glorious king, and the angels as soldiers conspicuous in varied attire: therefore we ask that, with reason searching, and suppressing with arguments whatever stands in the way, you bring forth to the light for us the truth that lies hidden as if in darkness, and that you set before the eyes of our heart God, who is to be seen one day, as you assert, made in some way visible.

MASTER. Since God almighty, alone immortal, alone invisible, alone incomprehensible, dwells in light inaccessible, while I, covered with the darkness of vices, dwell in foul gloom, unapproachable by the light of virtue: how shall I be able to bring the ineffable light to the wounded eyes of others, I who, with the eye of my heart half-blind, beaten back by the splendour of such great majesty, am in no way able to gaze on it?

DISC. Nevertheless strive as far as you can to be caught up into it, so that, the gloom dispelled, you may deserve to be illuminated by it, and we to be illumined through you; just as we often see valleys lit by the radiance of the Sun from the mountains.

MASTER. I will try as far as my strength allows, with you praying; and with logic going before and arguments accompanying, I will follow the truth as it flees even into the hiding place of its own inaccessible light, and, with its own consent, I will bring it forth to you as you search, showing itself.

DISC. Our prayer indeed will not fail you; only let reason, the guide to truth, go before you. For we greatly desire to hear from you how we ought to think about God in our prayers: lest perhaps the weak mind imagine for itself a handsome man, and, deceived, worship this image in place of the true God.

MASTER. I confess, overcome by the magnitude of the height of the business undertaken, I give way; for what I somehow conceive in the mind, I am scarcely able to unfold in words. For it far exceeds every illustrious genius of the greatest philosophers, since the sublimity of this matter which is treated surpasses all understanding. For the more, having entered into all creation, I try to contemplate it with careful gaze, the more I feel it withdraw from the sight of my understanding. Yet I will take pains to satisfy your inquiry according to my small measure, as far as he of whom we treat deigns to make the knowledge of himself known to the desiring soul. You, however, where my powers, pressed by the weight of so great a loftiness, give way, must pardon [my] frailty.

DISC. The more carefully we weigh the height of this matter, the more ardently we wish that it be made in some way knowable to us, and to gaze in whatever way on its beauty: and therefore we gladly pardon you if what you cannot [explain] in words, you explain at least by signs.

CHAPTER III. God cannot be properly expressed. None of the categories fits him. MASTER. It must be known, then, that God cannot be properly expressed by any words, nor comprehended by any thought. For how would he be declared immeasurable and incomprehensible, if he were enclosed in human speech or meditation? But now it is plain how wonderful he is, since he is unspeakable by all tongues and unthinkable by all hearts. For dialectic, mighty in disputation, powerfully defining every doubtful matter, brandishing and disembowelling all writings, reducing all human wisdom to nothing, when it turns towards the Godhead, beaten back by the light of such great majesty, turns back its fearful head trembling, and fleeing into the recesses of worldly wisdom hides itself, and, the bonds of its syllogisms dissolved, falls foolishly silent. For by noun and verb everything is expressed that is conceived by the human heart under the ten categories. But that none of these properly fits God, reason clearly proves. For if we say that God is a substance which grants subsistence to all things, and through which all things have being, at once universals and individuals, of which substance is predicated, the genera and species in which it is involved, and together the nine accidents which necessarily inhere in it, occur to the mind: all of which, it is clear, by no means apply to God. If we declare that God is magnitude itself, which disposes all things in measure and number and weight, immediately smallness sets itself against this quantity, and by its slightness diminishes what is greatest above all things. If we name him goodness itself, or the highest good, who makes all things very good, at once evil, contrary to this quality, meets [us], and does not fear to set itself against so great a good. But if he is declared Creator or Lord, each of which refers to something, namely to the world, at once relation objects that before the founding of the world he lacked this name, and that this relative [term] befell him from the creation of the world; whereas reason establishes that nothing in God is accidental, but that all that is predicated of him is essential to him. Further, if he is said to be wholly everywhere, and is said to fill all places at once, soon place, creeping in secretly, encloses in a place him who encloses all things in his fist. But if he is declared everlasting, and is affirmed to dispose all times, at once the present hastens to succeed the past, the future the present, and it does not fear to ascribe beginning and end to eternity. If, again, it is said that he possesses all things, and shines clothed with light as with a garment, at once thought deprives him of this having, while it separates from him the garment of light or the possession of things. But if he is testified to be always present, at once a position of standing or sitting is imagined. If, again, he is said to rule all things, the action of labour tries to annul eternal rest. Further, if he is affirmed to be patient, bearing our evils, immediately passion thrusts itself in, and maintains that the impassible suffers. For in these ten the whole human condition is enclosed, and from all of them the property of the highest essence is by evident reason wholly excluded. For all things that admit either opposition or contrariety or accident in no way properly fit God. Therefore, since with reason resisting we can say nothing properly of God, let us at least endeavour to speak of him improperly and in riddles.

CHAPTER IV. The mind is the mirror of the soul. Where knowledge comes to us from. Spiritual things are reached by faith, not by reason. 'Spirit' is used in six ways in Scripture. Air. Wind. The life of brute animals. DISC. Evident reason indeed teaches that God cannot be expressed in human words, but the intellectual mind eagerly desires that he be made in some way knowable to it; this mind seems to be like the mirror of the soul, in which it may contemplate the very image of its Creator.

MASTER. All that we know in created things we have come to know through the bodily senses. And those things which we have learned neither by sight nor by experience we learn through comparisons with things seen or experienced, as with what we read about beasts or unknown men; but things wholly unknown to us, if they are not signified through known comparisons, are never at all made known to our knowledge. And therefore, because spiritual things are invisible to us and not comparable with the bodily senses, they will never be provable to us by any reasoning. But because it is established that these things exist, yet they cannot be taught through likenesses, they require only the faith of those who believe.

DISC. What reason proves by arguments, even though they fall short in comparison, every rational person must not refuse to believe: only set out what reason indicates to you should be known about spirits.

MASTER. I am not unaware that you know that in the Scriptures 'spirit' is said substantially in six ways. First, the highest God of all is called spirit, as here: God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit (John 4:24). Second, angels are called spirits, as here: Who makes his angels spirits (Ps. 103:4). Third, souls are named spirits, as here: His spirit will go forth, and the flesh will return to the earth (Ps. 145:4). Fourth, the life of brute animals is called spirit, as here: Who knows whether the spirit of beasts goes down below? (Eccles. 3:21). Fifth, winds are called spirits, as here: The spirit of storms (Ps. 148:8). Sixth, air is written of as spirit, as here: I opened my mouth and drew in spirit (Ps. 118:131). Their definition is this: air is a spirit that is perceptible, not perceiving: that is, one which we perceive by drawing it in, while it perceives nothing itself, yet supplies breath to all that live under heaven. Wind is spirit, [that is] air stirred by some motion at God's bidding, increased by the storms of the waters, roused through the ministry of angels, and calmed through the same. The life of brute animals is a vital spirit consisting of air and blood, animal, invisible but perceiving, having memory but lacking understanding, dying with the flesh, vanishing into the air.

CHAPTER V. What the understanding soul is. It is a life that perceives, is changeable, not in a place, capable of suffering; without quantity, shape or colour. Now the soul is spirit, an incorporeal substance, the life of its body, invisible, perceiving, changeable, not in a place, capable of suffering, admitting neither the measure of quantities nor the form or colour of qualities: endowed with memory, rational, intellectual, immortal. And lest this definition waver, let reason strengthen it with proofs. The soul is a spiritual substance; for whatever supplies life to another must itself subsist: but the soul gives life to the body: therefore the soul really subsists. That it is life it itself proves, since by its presence it gives life to the body and by its absence puts the same to death. It is indeed invisible to us, but visible to spirits. It is also established that it perceives, since it enables the eyes to perceive colours, the ears sounds, the nostrils smells, the palate tastes, the hands rough or smooth things. It is also changeable: for whatever is made worse and made better is changeable; but the soul is made worse by vices and better by virtues; therefore it is changeable. It is also not in a place: for whatever is enclosed in a place, bounded in height, breadth and length of air, is a body; but reason has taught that the soul is incorporeal, that is, has neither a body nor any limb; therefore it is established that it is not in a place. For it does not occupy a space of air, as a body does, nor does it fill the body as water fills a wineskin; but as heat is present in the whole fire without place, so the soul fills the whole body without place. Fire indeed is visible, but heat is invisible and perceptible, and in a certain way gives life to the fire: so the soul, invisible but perceiving, by a certain hidden power gives sensation and life to the visible body. It is also capable of suffering: for whatever is affected by grief is capable of suffering: but the soul, when it is not made master of its will, is affected by the pain of sorrow; therefore it is shown to be capable of suffering. Quantity is excluded from it, since it is neither measured by height or breadth or length, nor does it allow the six surroundings, namely before and behind, right and left, above and below, to enclose it. The quality of form and colour is also separated from it, since no form, either of the human body or of any coloured thing, is ascribed to it. It is endowed with memory, because it recalls things past. It is rational, because it discerns things present. It is intellectual, because it understands things to come. That it is immortal is established from this, that it labours for the memory of itself to endure perpetually among those who come after.

CHAPTER VI. What angels are. Whether they exist. What they do. The difference between their knowledge and ours. Now an angel is spirit, an incorporeal substance, invisible, perceiving, rational, intellectual, immortal; [the substance] of the good ones bright and incapable of suffering, of the evil ones dark and capable of suffering. But it must be seen whether any such substance should be believed to exist among created things, since it is not seen by us at all. That angels exist is proved by the non-perceiving things themselves, which keep so fixed a law of their motion. For everything that is moved has its motion either from itself or from elsewhere: but everything that has its motion from itself perceives, like the soul; what [has it] from elsewhere does not perceive, like a body. Now if the sun, moon and stars are moved by themselves, they seem to flourish in sense or reason: for they keep such fixed times, such fixed tracts of the sky, and in a certain way indicate their understanding to this world by light or signs. But whoever judges them to be rational, or at least perceiving, bodies is rightly reckoned, as lacking sense, among irrational things. But since they are truly visible bodies, yet lacking [self-]motion, as being non-perceiving, and yet are moved, it is certainly established that they are moved from elsewhere. It remains, therefore, that they are moved through the ministry of angels. Likewise, whoever doubts that winds, rains, hail, lightning, thunder, storms and breezes are governed through them at God's command thinks these things perceive: but reason proves him a fool along with the non-perceiving things. Those too who do not believe that brute animals comply with or oppose human uses through them, or believe that the animals do this through the understanding of reason, depart far from reason. And whoever doubts that all that happens in non-perceiving things or in perceiving creatures is administered through them strays far from the light of truth. Therefore it is established that angels truly exist, and plainly know all things hidden from us. But there is this difference between their knowledge and ours, that they foreknow all the causes of things before they happen; but we scarcely, and with great labour, search them out after the things have come about in act.

CHAPTER VII. What God is. That he exists. That he is truth, life, wisdom, justice and eternity. Further, the highest spirit, just as he cannot properly be thought by any understanding, so he cannot properly be determined by any definition. But because the intellectual mind longs to come to know him in some way, let this riddling definition suffice it for the meantime. God is spirit, an invisible essence, incomprehensible to every creature, possessing essentially and all at once the whole of life, the whole of wisdom, the whole of eternity: or rather, existing as life itself, wisdom itself, truth itself, justice itself, eternity itself, containing every creature in himself like a point.

But if some fool is so foolish as to doubt that God exists, let him gather by this reasoning that he alone truly exists, and that all other things have their being from him. Every substance subsists either through itself or through another; but whoever contends that this world does not subsist, that idiot is heading for nothing. That the world does not subsist through itself is established, since reason teaches that it had a beginning; for it consists of parts. And everything that is joined from parts or resolved into parts certainly undergoes its joining or resolving from something. The world therefore does not subsist through itself; and so it follows that it is a creature. And a creature is referred to something, namely to a creator. Therefore the Creator alone exists through himself and in himself: but every creature subsists through him. For if he had being from another, then that from which he has it would be greater than God; which is unfitting to God. And since nothing exists besides the Creator and the creature, if God does not have being through himself, it follows of necessity that he exists through the creature; which is most unfitting. Moreover, the substance of the world is divided into various genera and into different species, and in each of these good is found. For everything useful is good: and all things are seen to be useful, and therefore each is proved good. And every good is good either through itself or through another. But the various goods must be good by participation in one good; for diversity admits more and less. For as regards genus, a stone is a lesser good, which only is and does not live; wood a greater good, which lives by growing; a horse better than that, which lives and perceives; a man more excellent than that, which lives, perceives, and discerns by reason. It remains therefore [that there is] a greatest and highest good beyond these, which is God, from whom as from a fountain all good things flow forth, and into whom all flow back.

He alone truly is; and therefore he is truth. For everything that is, is true, and what is not, is false; but God truly is, therefore he is truth. But the creature compared with him as it were is not: and therefore it is as falsehood to truth. For everything that began to be from nothing can be reduced to nothing: but every creature, brought forth by God from nothing, has been brought to be something: therefore, if it is compared with him, it is proved to be as nothing. So no mind doubts that God exists, through whom it sees that all other things exist. His essence is life. For everything that is either lives or lacks life; and everything that lives lives either through itself or through another: but God lives through himself and in himself, and has granted life to all others; therefore he is true life and living truth. He also knows and understands himself and all his handiwork, and for him to know is nothing other than to live and to be; therefore he is wisdom. He also loves himself and every creature; and he is justice: and he receives this justice from nowhere else; therefore he exists as justice and love. He lacks beginning and end, and has no past and future; therefore he is eternity.

CHAPTER VIII. How the brightness of God is to be known. That every soul is greater than the whole world. Intellectual magnitude. How the brightness of God is to be thought of. Since, then, reason has proved that God truly exists, and has taught by true assertions that he is essentially life, wisdom, truth, justice and eternity, it remains now that it should open some window for seeing him too, through which the mind, climbing by certain steps, may look out, so that it may be able to see the king of glory in his beauty. But let reason proceed step by step through bodily things, lest the weak understanding, straining through steep places, should be broken by the difficulty and slip back. First, then, let us consider in the mind this bodily sun, by whose greatness we see the whole world warmed, by whose brightness we see the whole earth lit. After this let us turn to the thousands of thousands of angels ministering to God, each of whom, as reason shows, we may know to be seven times, nay a hundred times, more splendid than the sun; for this sun is the servant of the world, but the angels are temples of God. As much, then, as the temple of God differs from the servant of the world, so much does the brightness of the angels differ from the brightness of the sun. Next let us weigh the ten thousand times hundreds of the sublime angels standing before God, each of whom we may know for certain to be a hundred times, nay a thousand times, brighter than the sun. For just as the moon is seen to excel the stars in brightness, and the sun the moon, so each higher order of angels is believed to surpass the lower in glory, dignity and brightness, from the Angels up to the Seraphim. After these let us look upon the countless thousands of holy souls, each of whom we do not doubt to be far brighter than the sun, to be made equal to the angels in blessedness and brightness. Having considered so many and such great lights one by one, let us also contemplate the greatness of each, so that we may more easily be raised up to that which we long to behold. Let us think, then, of the soul as a shining fire, whose least spark, as reason instructs, surpasses this sun, and moreover encloses the whole circuit of the world in a small space, while the whole earth by no means circumscribes it: therefore it is established that every soul [is] far [greater than] the whole world [...] magnitude of bodily quantity understands, but rather that intellectual [magnitude] which reduces this bodily world, and all the bodies in it, to smallness. From here now let the mind lift itself on high, let it widen its heart as far as it can, let it look out below itself upon so many lights shining with inestimable brightness and incomparable magnitude; and above itself let it gaze upon a certain wonderful light, which is the light of all those lights, which shines far above so many and such great lights as the sun shines above all the stars; whose ineffable magnitude and wonderful beauty those so many and such great lights continually wonder at, and into whose most abundant sweetness they delight to look without wearying. This surely is the light inaccessible, which the essence of God inhabits (1 Tim. 6:16), visible only to the pure in heart. Let no one here think of God as surrounded by light as a man by a tent, as if God who inhabits the light were one thing, and the light which he inhabits another: but rather let him know that the light itself is the essence of God, in which he may understand all good things to be placed at once. This is the light which satisfies angels and souls in heaven with the sight of it. This is [the light] which has provided the lamp of the sun to those dwelling in the world, like the light of a candle to those placed in prison; by which [they] may return from darkness to light, from death to life, from exile to the homeland [...] let your attention contemplate his image in this way, namely as such a light as shines above the sun as the sun above a candle; immortal, which shines above the countless thousands of angels and souls, a hundred times more splendid than the sun, as the sun above the stars. Hence he is called the Father of lights (James 1:17). For he does not stray far from the truth who keeps such an image of God before the eyes of the heart in prayer.

CHAPTER IX. The reason for the various names of the blessed vision of God. How the saints are to be thought of in prayer. This present vision of God face to face is called the kingdom of heaven, because outside this bodily heaven, nay outside every place, the angels and the just, who are called heavens, enjoy this vision. For this reason also, although God is believed to abide essentially in all creatures, he is said properly to dwell in the heavens, that is, in the just; because they perceive his indwelling by enjoying it, and rejoice to see that he is present in all things; while those who love earthly things know him to be by no means present to them. For just as when a seeing man and a blind man stand in the sun, the seeing man enjoys the brightness of the sun by seeing, the blind man is deprived of its light; and although the presence of the sun is equally there for both, yet each does not equally perceive its presence; so God is said to dwell only in those who enjoy his presence, either by seeing face to face, as the angels, or by beholding as in a mirror through contemplation, as the just in this life; but he is said not to be in those who are deprived of his vision. Hence also the kingdom of heaven is said to be within us (Luke 17:21), because the vision of almighty God, which is called the kingdom of the heavens, that is, of the just, is contemplated in the angels and the just. This is also called eternal life, because the blessed are fully steeped in the presence of unfailing life, and are never allowed to be subject either to death or to any pains, the servants of death. For they were created for this, that they might live eternally and eternally behold eternal life. This is also called the heavenly city, because the unanimous body of those citizens is gathered together to see the King of glory in his beauty. This is likewise named Jerusalem, because they are satisfied with the vision of ever-abiding peace. This is called paradise, because they rejoice in every kind of abundance of all delights. This is also named the homeland above, because all the just are not doubted to inherit this vision, as being sons of God. So when you call upon the saints in prayer, you ought to think of them thus: as set in the most bright glory of eternal brightness, that is, as most splendid lights shining far beyond the brilliance of the sun, who have all good things fully in the vision of God, and powerfully come to the help of all who call upon them.

DISCIPLES. May the eternal Sun, to the sight of whom your sweet discourse has led us, and whose serene light has shone in our hearts through your words, himself deliver you from darkness and set you in the region of light; and may he grant that you, shining among the lights you proclaim, may enjoy for ever the light of his vision.

MASTER. If anything worthy of approval is brought forth through me, I do not want it credited to me, but to God, whose gift it is; who often calls his sons to the inheritance of his vision through outcasts, and through enemies marks out beforehand for his friends the way of salvation from exile to the homeland. And you know well that sometimes an ugly man has held a mirror for a handsome one, nay a blind man a light for the seeing, and a lame man has shown the way to those sound of step.

CHAPTER X. That in God both a trinity of persons and a unity of essence are necessary. DISCIPLES. We too, for what we have heard, give thanks to the everlasting God, whose vision has been made known to us through you, and who through you has brought out for us such a treasure hidden from the carnal. But because the weight of the flesh burdens the soul, see, once more carnal thought knocks at the mind contemplating divine things. For since reason above has shown most truly that God is one, and has proved that he alone made all things from nothing, how are we taught to worship as it were three gods, when we are bidden to confess the Father perfect God, the Son perfect God, the Holy Spirit perfect God? For when three persons are thus distinguished as distinct, what else is understood by us than three gods?

MASTER. With truth itself showing itself and reason proving it, you will quickly see that a trinity of persons in one essence is necessary, and likewise that a unity of undivided substance is necessary for the three persons. When I spoke of God above in figures, because I could not speak in proper terms, what did I say the essence of God was?
DISCIPLES. Light.
MASTER. What is begotten from light?
DISCIPLES. Splendour.
MASTER. What is considered in light and splendour together?
DISCIPLES. Heat.
MASTER. Is any diversity found in the substance of light, splendour and heat?
DISCIPLES. No, but identity.
MASTER. Is identity predicated in their names or functions?
DISCIPLES. Not at all, but diversity; for the name 'light' seems to express the substance itself, the name 'splendour' the grace of light, and the name 'heat' the efficacy of light.
MASTER. So it is clear that three different names stand for one undivided essence.
DISCIPLES. It is clear in every way.

MASTER. You have it in the Apostle that the highest spirit, the Father, is called light: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). You have it in another Apostle that the highest Spirit, the Son, is also named splendour: Who is the splendour of his substance (Hebrews 1:3). You have it likewise in Moses that the highest Spirit, the Holy Spirit, is named heat: Our God is fire (Deuteronomy 4:24). So since light, splendour and heat are one nature and an undivided substance, but different in name, it is certainly established that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit have one nature and an undivided essence, since in what signifies what he is, he is substantially named spirit; and likewise that there is a necessary diversity in the persons, since the Father is proclaimed as begetting, the Son as being born, the Holy Spirit as proceeding from both.
DISCIPLES. We plainly perceive the trinity in the persons, and clearly hold the necessary unity in the substance.

CHAPTER XI. Why the names 'substance' and 'person' are said to be fitted to God. Why he is called Father and not mother. Why begetting. MASTER. These two names, namely substance and person, are fitted to the divine essence most carefully, because substance is always predicated of individuals existing in plurality, while person is predicated of an individual rational nature; for we are accustomed to designate plurality by 'persons', and unity of essence by 'substance'.
DISCIPLES. By what likeness is the eternal light called Father?
MASTER. Because from himself he begot offspring equal to himself.
DISCIPLES. Would not the name [mother] seem to suit him better?
MASTER. In the father there is always the principal cause of offspring, and therefore he rightly had to be called by this name, from the principal sex.

DISCIPLES. By what likeness is it said that he begets? MASTER. It is certain that [when] the mind thinks, it begets a thought; and when the mind thinks of itself, it generates as it were another like itself. So the highest God, when he thought of himself such as he is, without doubt generated an image like [him] in every way. And just as the one begetting is called Father, so the one begotten is most rightly named Son.

CHAPTER XII. That he never existed without the Son. DISCIPLES. If God begot the Son, it seems that there was a time when he did not have the Son, and that he possessed this name by accident. If that is so, the earlier statement is undermined, by which nothing accidental, but everything essential, was predicated of God.

MASTER. Reason has already taught that the essence of God is eternal life, knowing neither beginning nor end. If this unique true life always existed without beginning, it is established that without beginning it always understood that it lives. If it did not understand that it lives, it was not wise: which it is impious to say of God. If at some time it received wisdom from elsewhere, because it lacked it before, then that from which it received so great a good was better than God; which is utterly absurd. But if the everlasting life always understood that it lives, this wisdom of understanding did not come to it from elsewhere, but was always coessential with it, although it begot this from itself, as its offspring, ineffably. Therefore the Father never existed without the Son.
CHAPTER XIII. Why here a son, not a daughter. DISCIPLES. By what likeness is the splendour of the eternal light called Son, and not daughter?

MASTER. Because the likeness of the Father is expressed in him in every way, which is why he is also called his likeness. For nothing among created things fully keeps the likeness of that from which it is born. Hairs born from the head are unlike the head, fruits born from trees are unlike them, wool is unlike sheep; the young of animals, or even the children of men themselves, are not in every way like the quality of their parents. But this one is in every way most like the one begetting; and therefore most truly not a daughter, but a son.

CHAPTER XIV. Why 'Word'. The etymology of 'word'. DISCIPLES. By what relation is the Son called the Word? MASTER. A word is understood in three ways. For example, when this word, 'man', is uttered by the mouth; or when the same word, 'man', is formed in the heart without movement of the tongue; or when the thing itself which that word 'man' signifies is thought of in the understanding as it is. In this third way God begot his Word, when he spoke himself by thinking. And because by the same thought he spoke the whole form of the world, it is therefore said that he made all things in his Word: whence it is also read of the creation of the world, He spoke, and they were made (Psalm 32:9). For the Son or Word of God is nothing other than his thought, or art, or wisdom. Indeed, when we think of some thing, we form the image of that thing in our thought: so God, when he thought of himself, formed an image like himself in every way; and therefore this Word is called the image or likeness of God, but nothing other than the same essence is expressed. Hence too this 'verbum' is so called as if 'vere bonum' [truly good].
CHAPTER XV. That every created thing is life in the Word. DISCIPLES. How is it said, All that was made was life in him? Do stones, which are senseless, live in the Word of God?

MASTER. Every creature is said to subsist in three ways: in God, in itself, in us. In God [it is] unchangeable life, in itself changeable substance, in us an imaginable likeness of things. For example, a stone in itself is a changeable substance, because it can be turned into lime; in our thought [it is] the likeness of a stone. For when a craftsman thinks of making a house, the house already lives in the art itself, which the hand afterwards builds. But the one which the hand raises will fall; while the one which lives in the art endures. For the art is nothing other than the soul, and the soul nothing other than life: so the Word of God is nothing other than his art, and the art is nothing other than life itself: and in this all things will endure unchangeably which in their own substance are changeable and fail.

CHAPTER XVI. [Why] the Word alone could be incarnate. DISCIPLES. Since clear reason has proved irrefutably that the same Word, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one undivided substance, how could it alone be incarnate? For if it was separated from the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so became man singly, it is certainly established that the substance of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit is not undivided, since it could suffer the distinction of separation.

MASTER. Just as the everlasting power of the divinity can be understood through the things that are made and seen (Romans 1:20), so this exceedingly hidden depth can be looked into, with reason searching, through the things that take place in us. For it is known that the human mind begets from itself, by thinking, the word of common speech, and the same word exists at once in the mind and in the memory as one essence. But when the mind wishes to make its word known to others, it arranges, with the same thought, which is nothing other than its word, and with the memory, that the same word puts on the body of the voice, and goes forth audible to the ears and visible to the hearts of the hearers, and even allows its body to be bound in letters and seen; and yet, remaining invisible, it does not withdraw from the essence of the mind and memory. So it was not the mind nor the memory, but the word alone that sounded singly through the perceptible body of the voice; and yet it remained invisible, inseparably, in the essence of the mind and memory. So the highest Father begot his Word by thinking himself, and it subsists coessential in the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit together; but yet neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Word alone, which is the Son of the Father, singly put on a human body, showed itself perceptible to men, and allowed the body it had taken to suffer indignities; it itself remained inseparable, invisible and incapable of suffering in the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit.
CHAPTER XVII. Why the love of God [is called] Spirit, and why holy. DISCIPLES. By what likeness is the love of God called Spirit?

MASTER. I have said that the essence of God is life. True life understands that it lives; and if it understands itself to be life, it certainly loves itself. For God, to live, to understand and to love is nothing other than to exist. So the love of God is life, and life is spirit. And because God through love gives being or life to all things, he is therefore called spirit. And 'holy' is added because all things are made holy through him.

CHAPTER XVIII. How the Holy Spirit [proceeds] from the Father and the Son. In what way [he appeared] in the form of a dove or in fire. DISCIPLES. How is it proved that this Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son?

MASTER. The Holy Spirit is understood as nothing other than the love of God, which is also why God is called love (1 John 4:16). Now it is established that the Father loves the Son as himself; and likewise the Son loves the Father as himself; for life loves to be wise, and likewise wisdom loves to live: and it has been proved that life and wisdom are one essence. Therefore love, or affection, or charity, which is the Holy Spirit, exists coessential in the substance of the Father and the Son; and so proceeds equally from both.

DISCIPLES. If the Holy Spirit is coessential with the Father and the Son, how could he be separated from the undivided substance, when he appeared in the form of a dove above the Lord (Matthew 3:16), or in the form of fire above the apostles (Acts 2:3)?

MASTER. The substance of the Holy Spirit was not changed into a dove or fire, just as that of the Word was not transformed into flesh: but the Holy Spirit created the body of a dove, in which for a time he showed himself visible above the body of the Word, inseparably, as a testimony to men, while he himself remained invisible and inseparable in the essence of the Father and the Word. Possessing also the souls of the disciples inwardly, he showed outwardly the appearance of fire or light to the eyes of men as a sign, and yet did not withdraw from the substance of the Father [and] the Son; indicating, surely, that the Father and the Son consume sins through him, and that the hearts of men are kindled through him to love them; and that through him they will judge the wicked to the fire, but will glorify the just in him with the light of life.
CHAPTER XIX. On the equality of the persons. Why the deity is not worshipped under the names of the virtues. DISCIPLES. How is it established that these persons are equal?

MASTER. God is the highest life, the highest wisdom, the highest love. So as much as life lives, so much does it understand itself and so much does it love itself. For if it does not understand itself as much as it lives, it will by no means be the highest wisdom; and if it does not love itself as much as it understands itself, it is not the highest love at all. But since his substance is most truly the highest good, and the highest life and the highest wisdom and the highest love can be found nowhere but in the highest good, it necessarily follows that the three persons, of the Father begetting, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding, are equal in all things, and exist as the highest good in one and the same undivided substance.
DISCIPLES. Why is the deity venerated rather in these names, when mercy and justice and his other virtues are assigned to his essence?

MASTER. Because those belong to him properly and substantially according to himself, but these belong to him accidentally according to us. For he is called merciful not because he has a wretched heart; rather reason proves that all wretchedness is far from God. And human speech calls 'just' one who repays good to the good and evil to the evil. But because God comes to the aid of the wretched in their miseries, he has received the name of merciful or of mercy: although if there had never been anyone wretched on whom to bestow mercy, he would none the less be mercy itself in his own substance. And because he grants rewards to the just and inflicts just punishments on the unjust, he is justly called just or justice: yet if there were no one on whom to bestow either glory or punishment, he would none the less subsist as justice itself. So one should think of the other virtues.

CHAPTER XX. Whether some are necessarily wretched, and God then the author of evil. That the justice and mercy of God can be shown without wretchedness. DISCIPLES. Here a very great question seems to arise. If the mercy of God could not be discerned except through the wretched, nor his justice known except through those to be damned, it seems inevitably to follow that some were necessarily made wretched, through whom the mercy of God might be revealed, and some necessarily damnable, through whom the justice of God might be shown. If this is so, it will now be preached in vain that evil is nothing, since nothing worse can be thought of than wretchedness and damnation: and if this is not refuted by the strongest arguments of reason, then God is not at all known as the highest good, but rather is convicted of being the author of so great an evil. Further, if he was unwilling or unable to show his mercy except in the wretched, and his justice except in those to be damned, who does not see that it follows that he is either malevolent or powerless: in the one case, because he was unwilling to show good except through evil; in the other, because he could not do otherwise?

MASTER. Who, even if mad, would presume to say that the mercy and justice of God could not have been shown except through the wretched and those to be damned, when it is plainly established that we can display hidden riches not only through the needy but also through the well-off? For if I have hidden money, it will not therefore be necessary for some poor man to exist, by giving to whom I might make it manifest, since I can do the very same by giving to a rich man; but rather, if some poor man exists and comes to me, it will be fitting to bestow mercy on him from the hidden money. And so his experience proves me generous and wealthy; and it is established that the same can happen with a rich man, although the knowledge or experience of the poor man or the rich man brings me no benefit, since I possess all goods; but for them it is very profitable to know and experience that I have things useful, indeed necessary, to them. In just this way, if no one had ever been wretched or damnable, almighty God could none the less have shown mercy and justice in angels and men: namely, by mercifully granting them from his abundance what they did not have, especially since every creature has absolutely nothing of itself, but receives everything from him, the fount of all goods; and by justly preserving his gifts in his own, which they had received from him. And so it was not necessary that either an angel should fall into damnation to show God's justice, or man into wretchedness to declare God's mercy; since he declared both in the angels who stood firm: mercy, namely, by preserving them from falling; justice, by giving them rewards. But because angel and man apostatised from God by free will, they experienced openly mercy and justice, as if hidden before, when justice justly damned the one and mercy mercifully freed the other from wretchedness. And since no benefit accrued to God from this experience, in whom the fullness of all goods was before any creature was created, it follows that no necessity, but will alone, drove them to wretchedness.

CHAPTER XXI. That God is not the author of evil, but the one who orders it. The goodness of God. [His] omnipotence. That God is not the author of evil is plainly established by this: that he condemns all evil. Further, clear reason proves that evil does not subsist. For every substance is good, but evil is not good; therefore evil is not a substance, but is a privation of good. Evil seems to be a kind of separable accident of acting or of being acted upon: in action, when something is done in a disordered way; in being acted upon, when a disordered action is well ordered. For in the kingdom of him who orders all things nothing is left disordered. Now the right order of the rational creature is that it reject what is perishable and desire what will endure; that it love men, who are immortal in soul, and, loving God, the highest good, above all, obey his will. But those who despise the highest good, love the perishable good of the world, look down on their fellow souls and obey the desires of the flesh, live in a disordered way, and so do evil. But this evil will be ordered when this action is changed into being acted upon. For when such people are deprived both of the highest and of the perishable good of the world, they must be afflicted with harsh things, which are contrary to pleasures; yet these are not evil in themselves, but seem bitter to those who suffer them. Therefore by nature nothing is evil.

That God is the highest good is established by this: that he extends his mercy to the wicked and guilty, as if against justice. Indeed, from the fount of the highest good flows such a justice that by it God rightly ought to have mercy on the unworthy: and he is also proved benevolent in this, that he did not wish to enjoy so many goods alone, but brought forth from nothing so many substances, to which he distributed the goods of glory. And he is declared almighty, indeed omnipotence itself, by this: that he could form from nothing so great a fabric of things with all that exists, and that no creature bends him to anything unfitting, but whatever exists obeys his nod. See, the whole fortification of your proposition lies undermined by the battering-ram of manifest reason.

CHAPTER XXII. Whence created things come. Not from God's substance. Not from matter, but from nothing. Yet not from nothing. DISCIPLE: It is useful that the fortification of error be undermined and the citadel of truth be built. Since you have firmly laid its foundation upon him who creates all things, it remains for you to make the structure firm upon the origin of creation, to build it up by joining the end of the world to its beginning, and to complete its summit on the height of the kingdom of heaven. So, with reason as proof, make known to us whether the whole of creation was made from the Creator's substance, or from some pre-existing matter, or from nothing.

MASTER: The craftsman here has so strengthened the framework of this structure that no effort of any addition will shake his work. Creation itself denies that it is from the Creator's substance, and manifest reason fights against [this] with all its arms. For God is unchangeable, but every creature is changeable: if it had proceeded from an unchangeable nature, it would consequently itself endure unchangeable too. Further, if a corruptible nature came forth from God's substance, it follows that God's essence could be corrupted; the darts of reason pierce through this madness of a blind mind and cast it far from the presence of truth. That it was not made from any substantial matter is established by this: that nothing existed besides God. It remains, then, that the whole was created from nothing; not that nothing was or is something, but that what was not something, the Creator made to be this something. Yet before the creation the image of the whole of creation was in the Word, that is, in the art of God, after whose pattern the whole burst forth in creation. For just as a painter first shapes the variety of a painting in his mind, and afterwards paints a visible picture in its likeness, so God had first formed the whole of creation in his wisdom, and according to that form created all things in their manifold kinds. But the painter brings the picture conceived in his mind, which does not exist in reality, into being by means of colours and external instruments; whereas God brought forth the whole, [which was] in his wisdom, [without] instruments into so many substances; and therefore he made all things from nothing, and yet the visible world proceeded as if not from nothing but from something, since it put on forms after the likeness of the archetype.

CHAPTER XXIII. Questions on the presence of God. DISCIPLE: Now that the splendid tower is rising on high, let discerning reason drive out the darkness of error on every side, let it brighten the glorious structure with the clear light of truth, and let it reveal to us, as we marvel at the work of this famous building, whether the Creator is in creation, or creation in the Creator, or each in the other; or whether rather the Creator abides substantially somewhere outside creation in some glory, but fills creation by his power, reaching through it; whether half of him is in heaven and half in the world; whether he is sometimes wholly in heaven, sometimes wholly in the world; whether he exists divided through individual places, or whole in all places; whether he is sometimes in one place, sometimes in another, so that, for example, he should be believed to stay yesterday at Jerusalem, today at Carthage, tomorrow at Rome; or whether he is always and everywhere, outside every place and outside all time.

MASTER: Just as the rising sun by its presence lights up all the countless forms of things, however covered in darkness, so powerful reason, though your propositions are many and very tangled, examines them one by one with a keen gaze, and clearly sheds light on the deepest matters, drawn out of the darkest hiding places.

CHAPTER XXIV. That God is in every creature. That each perceives him to be in it. Every creature proves that the Creator exists in the whole of creation: it cries out that it has nothing from itself, but has its being and its good from God. For God is the highest essence and the highest good, and every creature subsists through him; every substance is good because it is; and where there is anything substantial, there God is: therefore God exists in every creature, since every creature subsists. Here perhaps a weak mind says to itself: If God is in every creature, then he is also in mud, and in hell, and in brute animals, indeed even in demons, which are certainly creatures. Here plain reason proves there is nothing unfitting, since it considers the good in all these. For mud is a thing mixed with another, such as earth with water or with something else of this kind: but earth is good because it is a substance, and water is good because it is a substance. Hell too is said to be fiery; and fire is good because it is a substance. Brute animals too are each useful for something in their kind, and therefore they are good. Demons likewise, in that they are of angelic nature, are good. Therefore, since it is established that each of these subsists in the good, does it not necessarily follow that God, who is goodness, is in all things?

But every creature also perceives through something that God is in it. For angels and all living things [perceive God to be in them, since they live through him; for God is life, and] whatever lives, lives by life. For an angel does not live more than a worm, though the one is immortal and the other mortal. Nor does an angel subsist more than a worm, although the substance of the one is eternal and of the other perishable. The heavenly bodies too, namely the sun, moon and stars, perceive God in them, since through him they shine and subsist. Trees and grasses perceive God in them, since through him they grow and subsist. Stones perceive God to be in them, since through him they subsist. Demons perceive God to be present to them, since through him they live and perceive; but they perceive God present also in this, that by God's just judgement they suffer evils in punishments. For God is justice, and wherever justice is exercised, God is believed to be there. So, in short, an emperor is present to a robber when he condemns him, just as to a soldier when he rewards him. And let no one suppose that God abhors the filth of the world, but let him know that he detests only the filth of sins; and that he can in no way be defiled by anything, just as a ray of the sun is not soiled by any uncleanness.

CHAPTER XXV. Creatures are also in God. An objection is resolved. A carnal thought about God and the world. A purer idea. That every creature exists in the Creator is known from this: that nothing is believed to be outside God; yet it is not in him in such a way that it is his substance or a part of him, as the heart is in an animal or is part of the animal, [but] as the light of a lamp in the sun is not its substance, nor part of its essence. But some fool bursts out here and says: If a stone is in God, and God is in a stone, then a stone is God. It certainly does not follow that everything which is in another is that in which it is; for wine is in a wineskin, and yet it is not the wineskin; the sun too is in a mirror, and the mirror in the sun, and yet neither is the other. Just as, if someone placed in Rome were to survey the whole city in thought, he would enclose the whole city with its people in his mind by imagining it; it would rightly be said that Rome is in his soul and his soul in Rome, and yet [Rome] would not be his substance: so indeed God is most rightly affirmed to be in every creature, and every creature in him, and yet neither is the other; but he is most truly declared the unchangeable Creator God, and it the changeable creature.

But because we were born in darkness, we cannot see the light of truth. We think of this world as founded upon the abyss, and of God as placed with the angels in heaven, and we suppose that outside this world there is nothing but darkness. But rather the sight of our mind is dulled by the greatness of the true light, as the bodily eye is dazzled by the brilliance of the sun, and our darkness does not comprehend such great brightness, and with the heart's gaze clouded it hinders us from contemplating it. Indeed, this whole world is gathered within God like the tiniest point, while the most serene light of his majesty is diffused outside on every side without measure. For God fills all things essentially, above and below, within and without, and round about; and the understanding of no creature exceeds his boundless substance by any thought. This again scandalises a weak understanding, and it turns over silently to itself: If all things are in God, then wolves and serpents, indeed demons too, are in him. Here, as above, nothing unfitting is proved, since good is found in all these. And every good is in God, outside whom there is nothing.

CHAPTER XXVI. Why not every creature enjoys the good equally, since every [creature] is in God. What it is to suffer evil. But it is asked why any creature suffers any evil, and why the whole [creation] does not rather enjoy the good equally, if God, who is the highest good, is declared to be in every creature. But it must be understood that, just as the soul, diffused through the whole body, is wholly present in each limb, yet does not grant to each limb all the functions of its governance, but to the eye only to see and not to hear, to the ear to hear and not to see, and to the rest in this manner; and the limb from which it withdraws the gift of life will remain senseless and useless in the body, and this is said to suffer evil or nothing, because it is deprived of good: so God, diffused through all things, is wholly present in each, yet does not grant to each all the gifts of his grace, but to each as it pleases him: to a stone only to be and not to live, to a tree to live by growing [but] not to perceive, to beasts to perceive [but] not to discern, to angels and souls to discern and to exist immortal. And whatever he withdraws any of these from will at once be useless in the body of the universe. And when the good which is pleasing to its nature is withdrawn from it, it is soon of necessity affected by the bitterness which is contrary to it, as men in the world, demons in hell: and so it is said to suffer evil while it is deprived of good, just as a blind man placed in the sun is said to suffer darkness, because he does not enjoy its light. But why God offers to one creature the sweetness of his presence to enjoy and withdraws it from another, reason cannot penetrate with any sharpness, but stands in awe of God, terrible in his judgements.

CHAPTER XXVII. Why things change, when they are in the unchangeable. Again it is asked: if God is in every creature, and every creature is in him, how does anything fail, and why does the whole not rather remain in one state, especially since the unchangeable God contains all things? But it must be understood that by this the Creator is distinguished from the creature, since he is seen to be unchangeable, but it very unstable; yet all things imitate eternity, since by failing and growing again they are always turned as if in circles of existence. For because they took their origin from nothing, they desire to run back into nothing and, as it were, to go out of God. But because they find no way out, they return again into being as if turned back in circles. The heavens and stars are always revolved in their circles; waters, by flowing continually, return to their springs as if a circle had been completed. Trees, grasses, animals, by growing, ageing, rotting and growing again, are in a certain way driven round in a circle. In this way too all things of themselves tend towards nothing, but through the one who holds them together they always strive to return to the nature given [them]. Again it is asked: if man had stood firm in paradise, would all these things have been changeable as now? Without doubt all things, with passing time, as now, would have kept their alternations by growing, failing, being born and dying; he himself would have endured stable in one state and lord of all. But because by sinning he became unstable, he himself began to slip away with time and perishable things.

CHAPTER XXVIII. Whether, had man not sinned, they would have been changeable. That God is everywhere, and how. Now that the darkness has been driven from the structure of the sacred building, let us gird ourselves to dismantle the engines raised against it. That God is somewhere substantially and everywhere potentially is opposed to the firmness of the whole disputation already worked out, and is overthrown by the thrust of most evident reason. For if he is substantially somewhere and not everywhere, then he is circumscribed and in a place; and if he is in a place, then he is a body; and if he is a body, it is concluded that he is not God. Further, if God is contained by a place, then the place which contains him is greater and better than he: greater, because it encloses God; better, because it contains so great a good. Moreover, if he is substantially in heaven but potentially in the world, then his essence is one thing and his power another; and it follows that this power has come to him as an accident, which reason drove away above from the face of truth. But if he is half in heaven and half in the world, then the creature contains the Creator and encloses its maker within itself. But if he is sometimes in heaven, sometimes in the world, then he is proved changeable, because he is moved from place to place. Further, if God is sometimes in heaven and not in the world, then there is something only where he himself is, and elsewhere there is nothing; for where God is not, there is nothing. But if he is divided through the individual places, then he consists of parts; and it follows that he who is divisible through places is capable of suffering, and also dissoluble: for everything which consists of parts can be dissolved. But if he is whole in each place, then there are as many wholes as there are places; for of everything which is wholly enclosed in one place, no part is shown to be in another place; and it follows that God is enclosed by place, he who is proclaimed to enclose all things in his fist. And if he is changed through the alternations of times, and stays yesterday in one place, today in another, tomorrow in a third, then he is temporal: and he has already lost the past, does not yet have the future, and moreover all accidents converge upon him.

CHAPTER XXIX. Conclusion of the questions on the presence of God. A comparison. The instruments of the sacred tower easily dismantle the engines of this most false opinion. God's power is nothing other than his essence: therefore God is not somewhere determinately, but everywhere essentially. God is also immeasurable; but place, namely the space which any body occupies, is measured by height, breadth and length, and whatever is in a place is circumscribed by above and below: therefore God is neither partly in [heaven] nor partly in the world; nor sometimes wholly in heaven, sometimes wholly in the world; nor divided through individual places, nor wholly in each separately; but existing outside every place in himself and through himself, filling every place and containing it in himself, penetrating all creation, holding the universe together through his substance, namely everywhere, in all things and outside all things, whole, and removed from no place. Just as the light of a lamp shines wholly in the eyes of all who stand around, and remains wholly in itself; it does not withdraw from itself to reach those present, nor leave one to shine for another, but rather shines wholly for each and all at once, and remains wholly in itself: so God is whole everywhere and in all things, and remains whole in himself; he does not withdraw from himself, but gathers all things into himself.

CHAPTER XXX. How Christ [was] wholly in heaven, wholly in the Virgin's womb. Hence it is asked, since God is not enclosed by place, how Christ is proclaimed wholly in the Virgin's womb and wholly in heaven, since the Virgin's womb is undoubtedly a place. In heaven he was wholly in the Father's essence, as all wisdom is in the soul; in the Virgin's womb [he was] wholly, as the whole word is in the voice. For God lacks beginning and end; and therefore he remains eternal. So he neither was past, [nor will be future, but] is present, existing always and everywhere; hence he is also named 'Is' (Exod. 3:14); because, existing as eternity and disposing all times, he is varied by no time. See, the engine of your manifold proposition collapses, because no accident converges upon God.

CHAPTER XXXI. How God alone is immortal. How alone invisible. It was said above that God alone is immortal, alone invisible. Are angels or souls mortal, then, or is God invisible to the angels, of whom it is said that they always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10)?

MASTER. Changeability is a kind of mortality: for while something is moved from past into future, it as it were dies to the past. God alone is unchangeable, because nothing of the past departs from him, nothing of the future comes to him, but whatever is or was or will be is always wholly present to him; and just as it cannot be thought that he ever had a beginning, so too it cannot be thought that he could ever be ended. But angels are changeable, because they are moved from past into present, from present into future; for they lack the past and do not yet have the future. For it is certain that they do not have the angelic companions lost long ago, and that they still lack the fellowship of the saints on pilgrimage on earth. They gather the past by memory, they understand the future by foreknowing it. And just as it can be thought that they once began, so too it can be thought that they could be ended. And moreover, when they consider created things changeable in themselves, they in a certain way fall away from the state of unchangeability: such changeability is for them a kind of mortality. Souls, however, just as they are changeable in all respects, so too are almost in all respects mortal. For God is the life of the soul, as it is the life of the body: but just as the body is dead when it does not have the soul, so the soul is dead when it lacks God; or just as a blind eye is called dead when it is deprived of light, so the soul [is] dead when it does not enjoy the blessed life, which is God. God alone therefore has immortality, because he admits no changeability. He alone is also invisible, because he is not fully intelligible to any creature. Indeed angels [and] the souls of the blessed always see him in their own way, not in ours; not across intervals of space, as we see bodily things, but within themselves and outside themselves, in every creature and outside every creature they behold him, and by no gaze of the understanding do they exceed the amplitude of his brightness. And because he is not fully seen or understood by them as he is by himself, therefore he alone is called invisible.

CHAPTER XXXII. How far man [was] created in the image and likeness of God. Every thing has some likeness of God. That souls are eternal. Disc. Now that the divine nature, together with the angelic, holds the sceptre in this tower, see, human nature brings up a legion and raises an engine to assault it. For it is asked how man is said to have been formed in the image and likeness of God, when no correspondence and likeness to God is seen in man.

MAST. Assailants are overcome by opponents, while what goes before is made impregnably strong by what follows. Two men are written of, the inner and the outer. The inner is the soul, the outer the body; the inner invisible, the outer visible. So the invisible [man] was created in the image and likeness of the invisible God, but the visible was formed after the visible world. The invisible God is unity in substance, trinity in persons. So the inner man, that is, the soul, was created in the image of the unity, because it is not composed of parts like the body, but is a simple nature and an immortal essence. God is also memory, which remembers itself and all things that are, which is named the Father: from it is born understanding, which understands itself and all things that are, which is called the Son: from both proceeds love, which loves itself and all things that are, which is called the Holy Spirit. The soul is made in the image of this Trinity, when memory, understanding, and the reason of love are placed in it; for it remembers things past, understands invisible things, and rejecting evil loves good. The essence of God is also light, life, justice, goodness, blessedness. The soul was made in this likeness, so as to be bright, living, just, good, blessed. But the outer man, that is, the body, is formed in a certain way on the pattern of the world, since it is put together from four elements: hence it is also named microcosm, that is, lesser world. And in this too the soul has a likeness of God, since it governs the lesser world as God [governs] the greater. Every creature also has a likeness of God in some respect, and the more excellent each is than another, the more like him it is. For he is, lives, perceives, discerns by reason. Stones therefore attach themselves to his likeness, because they are. Trees come nearer to his likeness, because they are, and live by growing. All animals express his likeness much more, because they are, live and perceive. Further, in men and angels the likeness of God shines out most, because they are, live, perceive and discern by reason.

It is established that souls are eternal. For if they are proclaimed to have been made to see God, it follows necessarily that, just as God is believed to have no end, so it should not be doubted that the souls who will see him live without end. But it is asked whether those souls are immortal which will not see God. It is established that all souls are of one nature; and if some souls are immortal, then all are immortal: therefore all souls that will see God will be blessed forever, and those that will not see him wretched forever.
CHAPTER XXXIII. Whence the soul sees so many things in dreams. Why it does not see itself. Disc. Whence do souls see so much in dreams?

MAST. The soul is gripped by an insatiable desire to know the truth, and so it always wanders in thoughts; and so, when the bodily senses are asleep, it foresees future things through certain riddles as God reveals them, [and] sometimes it languishes anxiously over likely-seeming things as the devil deceives [it]: sometimes it converses with angels or souls, sometimes it is mocked by demons. In the manner of the eye, it sees all other things, [but cannot] see itself.
Disc. Why is it not seen by us?

MAST. Because its nature is said to be so fine that it does not allow itself to be seen by bodily eyes. For as much as water is thinner than earth, so much finer is air than water; and as much as the ethereal fire [surpasses] air in thinness, so much does the soul surpass heavenly fire in fineness. This is the reason why no spirit is seen by us, because the fineness of their nature is believed to exceed our sight.

CHAPTER XXXIV. How it is whole in each limb. Disc. How is the soul said to be spread through the whole body, and yet to be no more in the largest and no less in the smallest limbs, but whole in each? Are there then as many wholes as limbs?

MAST. As was said above, if a light is placed in the middle, it shines no less in my eyes and no more in another's, but whole in each, and remains whole in itself; so the soul is everywhere in the body and whole in each limb; hence when one limb is touched the whole [soul] feels pain. Yet there are not as many wholes as limbs, because it remains whole in itself; just as a voice sounds in the ears of all not in part but whole, and remains whole in itself.
