CHAPTER XXXV. Why one [soul] is more capable of learning than another. Disc. If all souls are of one nature, what is the reason that one is more apt, another slower, at learning?

MAST. The soul has the form of wax or of a candle. Wax is apt to express an image if a seal is pressed on it; so a candle [is apt] to give light if it is lit. In this way the soul expresses the image of knowledge if the seal of teaching is pressed on it, and receives the light of truth if it has been lit by the fire of wisdom: but if it neglects to make itself apt through study or exercise, then, like wax without an image and like an unlit candle without light, it will remain in the darkness of ignorance without knowledge and truth. The more each soul adapts itself to teaching, the more capable of knowledge it will be. But why the fire of the Holy Spirit lights some souls that do not make themselves apt, indeed are negligent, more with the light of knowledge, and does not light others; indeed why it withdraws knowledge from some who labour, and does not withdraw it from others like them: reason, unable to penetrate [this], cries out in wonder: O how incomprehensible are the judgements of God, and his ways unsearchable (Rom. 11:33)!

CHAPTER XXXVI. That we have one master. Disc. Since all things are learned from masters, how is it written that there is one master in heaven (Matt. 23:8–10), by whom, as it were, each thing is especially taught?

MAST. If it is rightly weighed, nothing at all is learned through a man. Masters only plant and water outside by reminding the soul; but the truth that dwells in the soul gives the increase by teaching within (1 Cor. 3:7). But folly does not understand these things: reason, however, which discerns all things, will easily prove that they are so. Indeed whatever is learned is grasped better by sight than by hearing. For however much I tell one born blind about the sun, he still does not know what the sun is, which he has never seen; he only believes from my words that there is something called by that name, or perhaps doubts that anything really exists that is so named: but if he should suddenly see, by the very sight he proves that the sun exists, which he could not know by hearing. So many blind people know the Scriptures, yet do not know what a book or a letter is; if their eyes were suddenly opened and a book were placed before them, they would wonder what it is they see, and discern by sight what they could not by hearing. Further, if I say to one of them, 'Such a letter is called A, and such is named B', he at once turns back inward, consults the truth, and proves that what he hears is true. What then did I teach this man, who could know what a letter was neither before by hearing nor afterwards by sight, unless he learned it with truth teaching within and sight confirming outside? I only uttered the sounds of words; but he came to know the words and the things signified by the words, with truth examining within. So you too, if I tell you much about the elephant, do not know what an elephant is unless you see it; so we read much about David, and know him as it were as a red-haired man and handsome to look at; if he came in now, would we recognise him? I think not at all. Why? Because we could not learn from masters what we have not proved by the truth of sight. For teachers only utter the sounds of words; but hearers, with truth teaching within, learn the words by the mind, the things by sight. So we learn letters, so unknown languages, so various arts: we receive the sounds of words from teachers, [and] consider the things themselves within, with truth teaching. But what is to be said of song, which is not seen but learned only by hearing? Is it not that, while the singer's voice sounds outside, truth forms within the soul certain ascents, as it were, of the voice? Therefore nothing at all but sound alone is learned through a man; but words and things are discerned through the truth dwelling in the inner man. And so most truly one master is proclaimed, by whom each person is instructed inwardly. But those things which are not seen by us, such as God and the angels, are only believed to exist.
CHAPTER XXXVII. What the difference is between believing God and believing in God. True faith. DISC. Is there any difference between believing God and believing in God?

MAST. A great deal. For demons and pagans believe God, but they do not believe in God. For they believe that there is a God who created all things and is powerful over all things. But only those believe in God who, by loving him, strive towards him. True faith is to believe that God is unity in essence and trinity in persons, and that he created all things from nothing by his Word, and restored what had fallen by that same Word incarnate, and on the last day will renew all things through his Spirit; and that to those who believe this he will give the highest good, namely himself, as a reward. This faith is the life of the soul, and by it the just man lives. This faith is nourished by hope, as the body is refreshed by food; it is given life by love, as the body is quickened by the soul; and love is proved by deeds, which is why faith without works is declared dead (James 2:17). So by faith the soul turns away from evil and does good; by hope it spurns all passing things and longs for invisible things like itself; by love it endures every hardship, reins in the urges of the flesh, gives out what is needed to its neighbours, and always yearns for the highest good. Therefore the soul that strives towards God by believing and hoping in this way will possess the highest good itself without end.

CHAPTER XXXVIII. That souls freed from the flesh perceive nothing corporeal. DISC. If souls are by nature bright, the question is whether the light of day gives anything to souls exiled from the body, or again whether the darkness of night does any harm to their seeing?

MAST. Just as a body without a soul is seen to perceive nothing, so we believe that a soul without a body certainly perceives nothing corporeal. For when mingled with the body it perceives colours through the eyes, sounds through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the palate, and tangible things differing in softness or hardness through touch or walking. But when separated from the body it perceives nothing corporeal in a corporeal way; it beholds each thing in the property of its substance, with the accidents of colour removed, and it also perceives spiritual things in its own manner. So just as the light of a candle gives nothing to the sun for shining, so the light of the sun certainly gives nothing at all to the soul for seeing. And just as night does not hinder the radiance of the sun, but rather flees from it, so neither does it stand in the soul's way at all, since the soul does not even perceive it. Moreover, the soul either enjoys spiritual light, being itself far brighter than the sun, or, darkened by the dreadful gloom of sins, is wrapped like a blind man not in the darkness of night but in its own. That the soul freed from the flesh does not see light in a corporeal way is clear from this: when we want to compose something, or plan to do something, the soul at once flees the outward senses, gathers itself inward, and considers within itself the things it is dealing with; and the light of the sun is of no use to it, but even hinders it in this business; and while it attends elsewhere, it does not hear loud voices beside it. Therefore the soul outside the body sees or hears nothing corporeal. And if it does so, then it has certainly put on an airy body.

CHAPTER XXXIX. Which saints hear our prayers. Disc. If souls do not hear corporeal voices, how is it that many have found that the souls of the saints, for instance of Peter or Martin or another, have heard their prayers?

MAST. The prayer of the heart, not of the mouth, ascends to heaven. For souls hear not the cry of the voice but of the heart, and they come to the aid of those who call on them faithfully. Nor do they hear loud prayers more than those made without voice, either on the tongue or in the heart alone; for even by us it is not words but only sounds that are heard; words, rather, are seen by the mind. So when our souls desire something in accordance with God, and ask, whether by heart, by tongue, or by voice, that it be given them by God through the saints, the souls of the saints (for whom hearing is the same as seeing, and the other way round), beholding not the sounds but the words, obtain for them from God what they desired; which is why you have it written: The Lord has heard the desire of the poor (Ps. 10:17, according to the Hebrew).

CHAPTER XL. How it is to be understood that a soul is released from the body and returns again and reports what it saw. Hell is incorporeal, or else damned souls put on a body. DISC. Do we not read that many souls, often, having been led out of the body, saw many places of punishment, and likewise many pleasant and flowering places, and in both of them many souls in human form, and that on returning to the body they reported that they had heard very many things from them?

MAST. It must be understood that these souls had not left the body entirely, but had only released the bodily senses from their functions, and the body was not wholly without the vital spirit. Hence the things they had heard were not corporeal things but likenesses of corporeal things, which on returning they could report to others still in the body for their edification. But once they had put off the body completely, the matter was far otherwise than they had been able to see before. Just as we, sometimes, standing beside a wall, see the shadow of a man coming, not the man himself; but when the obstacle of the wall is removed we see him as he is. Also, when the souls of the dead appear to the living, they put on an airy body, in which they produce a corporeal voice or audible words.

From this it is gathered that hell is incorporeal, a spiritual substance resembling a corporeal one; and its punishment is as much more unbearable as spirit is subtler than body. For every body fails with age, and, dissolved by long duration, will perish. So if the fire of hell is corporeal, it follows that it is fed by corporeal fuel, and it follows that when that is consumed it will itself perish; but it is agreed that the fire of Gehenna does not fail; therefore it is spiritual. But if it is corporeal, yet created unfailing, then souls and spirits must put on some kind of body in which to feel that corporeal fire.

CHAPTER XLI. Proof of the resurrection of the dead drawn from the promises of God. Another from the eternity of souls. The new creation is spoken of in three ways. Disc. Can the resurrection of the dead be proved by reason?

MAST. If those things stand unshaken which were proved above by most true arguments, then, with every objection removed and every necessity applied, the resurrection will come. For it has been established that God is truth; and the words of truth must be fulfilled; for if they are not fulfilled, it follows that either God is changeable or he is not truth; and if they cannot be fulfilled, then God is not almighty. It is plain how utterly absurd all these things are with respect to God. So God, the unchangeable truth, has promised full joy to those who love him and full punishment to those who scorn him, and both will be impossible unless it is in soul and body; it is necessary, therefore, that bodies rise again and receive their souls, so that, according to the promises of the Truth, the former may have full joy in soul and body, and the latter receive full punishment in the same way. Further, if bodies do not rise, then souls were not made eternal; but it was proved above that souls were made eternal, made, that is, for this purpose, that they might always see God with the angels and in this vision live blessedly without end. But they do not live blessedly if they see their garments, that is, their bodies, rotting in filth without hope of recovery. It follows, therefore, that necessarily the garments of holy souls, which are called robes, are renewed through the resurrection and changed into incorruptible glory, so that the souls clothed in them may contemplate God, ever blessed; and conversely that the unhappy ones put on again their filthy garments, at whose foulness they may grieve for ever. Therefore not only must bodies be renewed, but the common nature too, which has served the saints, must be changed for the better; which is why you have it written: Behold, I make all things new (Rev. 21:5).
Disc. Since God, from the beginning of the world until now, has created nothing new, how will it be established that there is a new creation?

MAST. The new creation is spoken of in three ways, which are arranged thus through the Trinity. God the Father founded every creature from nothing, and this is called a new creation. God the Son, too, incarnate, established the Church with a new religion, and it is called a new creation; which is why you have in the Apostle: We are a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17); and in another: That we might be a beginning of his creation (James 1:18). God the Holy Spirit, too, will yet give life to bodies and renew the whole world; and this too is called a new creation; which is why you have: The Lord will make a new heaven and a new earth (Isa. 65:17).

CHAPTER XLII. How Christ or the saints are in heaven. What is commonly understood by the name of heaven. That the eyes do not reach the firmament. Disc. Now that the tower has been nobly carried up to the top, it remains for it to be girded with battlements, and so for its summit to be completed at the height of the heavens. We read of the Lord that with hands raised he was carried into heaven, and that he sits at the right hand of God (Luke 24:50; Mark 16:19); and Stephen, in the assembly, saw him standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). Whatever is carried from place to place is moved; and whatever sits or stands is contained by a place. And since the Lord ascended into heaven bodily, we greatly desire to know how he is now to be believed to be there, or how the souls of the saints are now there, or how they will be there once they have received their bodies. For if some place holds Christ or the saints, sitting or standing, so that they do not fall, then that place is proved better than they, since so many good beings are held by it. And if the saints rejoice and glory in some visible and perceptible creature, as we take delight in this visible and perceptible light, then again that thing is judged better than the rational creature, which delights in possessing it, as we rejoice in money we have; and it seems a wretched joy if an intellectual creature rejoices only in a senseless thing.

MAST. Let us climb together to the top of this tower, and, with reason searching it out, let us look closely at how these things stand. By the customary name we call 'heaven' what we see above our head. Above us, however, we observe nothing but clouds, or air lit by the sun. The sun, or the moon, or the stars, far removed from us, we see in the way that, when placed on the wide sea, we observe mountains from far off, while all around we discern nothing but the air poured about us. From this it is clear that no man's sight penetrates the whole extent of this air, since it can scarcely even reach the horizon. Hence, when the apostles could no longer see the Lord once he was taken up, it is said: A cloud received him out of their sight (Acts 1:9). Stephen, too, did not see the Lord in heaven beyond the firmament with bodily eyes, since no man's sight can in any way reach as far as the firmament. Moreover, that assembly in which Stephen, standing, beheld Christ (Acts 7:55) was in some house, the top of whose roof his bodily eye could by no means penetrate. It is established, therefore, that he saw Christ not with the eye of the body but with the gaze of the inner man, and not in a bodily heaven but in an intellectual heaven. But here perhaps some quibblers object that the stars are fixed in the firmament, and that our sight reaches the firmament when we see them. Do our eyes reach the firmament, then, because they look at the stars? Do they penetrate the whole extent of the air at sea, because they observe the mountains, that is, solid bodies? For just as at sea, when the mountains are removed from view, nothing but air is seen on every side, so too, when the stars, that is, solid bodies, are taken away, nothing but air is discerned. But whatever lies from the air up to the firmament, and the firmament itself, is in no way seen by us, because of the great distance of that space, and because of the subtlety of its nature.

CHAPTER XLIII. Heaven threefold in the literal sense. Three heavens signifying three visions. The apostle's rapture to the third heaven. Why angels and the just are called heavens, and demons darkness. But if perhaps it is objected that the Apostle is written to have been caught up to the third heaven, it must be known that three heavens are named in the literal sense, and again three are so called in a figurative sense. This air, indeed, is called the first heaven in the literal sense, as you have: The birds of heaven, because they are seen to fly in heaven, that is, in the air. The second heaven is named the ether, as you have: The stars of heaven, because the planets are borne there in their wandering course. The third heaven is called the firmament, as you have: The constellations of heaven, because the stars are said to be fixed in it. Three heavens are also read of in a figurative sense, because three visions, namely sensory, spiritual, and intellectual, are not unknown to the wise. Sensory vision is when we discern the colours and forms of things outwardly, but understand that something is hidden within, as we understand the meaning in letters. This vision, then, is named the first, the sensory heaven, because understanding is hidden in the scriptures. For heaven (caelum) takes its name from hiding (celare). The second vision is spiritual, by which we see in spirit not things but images like things, as we are accustomed to in dreams, and as we know John in the Apocalypse and the prophets saw many things; and this vision is called the second heaven, because the true things are hidden in these likenesses. The third vision is intellectual, when we behold with the intellect neither things outwardly nor images of things inwardly, but the substances themselves as they truly are, with colours abstracted, and by reason discern the quality of each, as it differs from the others; and this vision is called the third heaven, because the truth of things is hidden in it from fools, as if in heaven. If, therefore, the Apostle was caught up in the body, then he was brought to the bodily heaven, namely the firmament; but if outside the body, which seems more likely, then he is certainly believed to have been caught up to the intellectual heaven, in which he is known to have seen the essence of the Godhead as it is, and the angelic substances as they are, not sensorily, which cannot happen except through the body, nor spiritually, which does not happen except through images like things, but truly, which does not happen except by the intellect itself. Angels or the just are called heavens by a certain likeness, because in the secret place of God they are hidden from human sight; and conversely demons or the wicked are called darkness, because in torments they are hidden from us.

CHAPTER XLIV. What the kingdom of heaven is, and that it is everywhere. Why we are not now in heaven. What it is to enter it. What [it is] to be carried in. For what purpose bodily visions are granted to some who are dying. The kingdom of heaven, that is, of the just, is believed to be not the walls of cities, not estates of possessions, not an abundance of gold and gems, not varied furnishings, but justice and peace and glory of every kind in full joy, which is had from the vision of eternal brightness and from the company of the angels and saints. God, the eternal light, has been proved to be in the world and outside the world, below and above and round about, on every side and everywhere. If, therefore, the kingdom of heaven, as reason shows, is nothing other than the vision of God, who is the fount of all goods, it necessarily follows that the kingdom of heaven is in this world and outside the world, and in every creature and outside every creature; which is why you have: The kingdom of heaven is within you (Luke 17:21); because, of course, abiding in God, we behold him as he is in ourselves, and in every creature, and outside every creature. We are said now to be outside God, or outside the kingdom of heaven, for this reason: because we are deprived of this vision. In the same way the wretched are said to be shut out then from the kingdom of heaven, because they will be deprived of that same vision, as the blind are of the light of the sun. The just are written to enter this kingdom of heaven, or this joy, because, unable to contain the ineffable joy, they are in a certain way wrapped up in it. That souls are asserted to be carried upward to heaven, or are even thought to be carried in, is said with reference to our sight, to whom higher things are known as brighter with the splendour of the sun, and because this matter cannot otherwise be grasped by those who are still set in the flesh. Truly, souls released from the flesh are not moved in place, nor led into some bodily place so as to contemplate God from there; but as soon as they are separated from the body, they are joined to the angels and saints, and without delay enjoy the kingdom of heaven, which is the vision of God, within the world and outside it and everywhere: just as a blind man set in the sun, if his eyes were opened, would at once enjoy the light of the sun. That to some who are dying light or the forms of angels or saints are seen there, and concerts of harmony are heard, and they are seen to be led on high, this undoubtedly happens for the sake of the living, so that they may be strengthened in the Christian religion. Further, it seems frivolous if souls, which are not in a place, are asserted to be led from this world beyond the firmament, as if it were more beautiful there, or God were more there, when rather God is proved to be present equally above and below, within and without. That souls, since they are incorporeal spirits, should be enclosed in bodily places seems most absurd, especially since every place is measured by height, length, and breadth, and spirit is well known to lack all these. They are thought, rather, to abide in him without place and to enjoy the vision of him, just as knowledge dwells in the soul without place.

CHAPTER XLV. The glory and place of the bodies of the blessed. The twinkling of an eye. The body of the saints will rise spiritual, because in lightness, swiftness, and transparency it will be equal to spirits, and every solid thing will be penetrable to it; just as the body of the Lord also rose though closed in by a stone, and entered though the doors were shut. Just as, then, spirit is now sustained by no bodily place, so too it is not necessary that the spiritual body then be propped up by any place. For the non-perceiving body does not quicken the spirit, but the spirit the body. Therefore no place props up the spiritual body, which will be subtler than every element, but, like spirit, it subsists without place in God, the highest spirit; unless perhaps that is taken for a place which is circumscribed substantially and personally. Further, either the saints will see God while remaining in this bodily world, or they will be outside the world. If they are outside the world, then, standing or sitting, they are sustained by no elemental matter, because no element is shown to exist outside the world. For whoever believes that earth or water is there is foolish, being too earthly and fluid; and if anyone thinks that air or fire is there, he is reckoned, being himself unstable from the mobility of air and fire, a grave laughing-stock. Therefore outside the world they are propped up by no material thing, where none is found. But if they are in this world, likewise they will cling to no element locally by standing or sitting, because they will be equal to the angels (Matt. 22:30). Since, then, they are spiritual, they will abide in the highest spirit spiritually, not locally. Further, the glory of those bodies is to be contemplated not by reason but by faith alone. For then those bodies will be agile as the mind, transparent as the sun. As swiftly as the mind now reaches from East to West in thought, so swiftly will that body then be able to reach there. This is gathered from the fact that the resurrection is read to take place in the twinkling of an eye (1 Cor. 15:52). The twinkling of an eye, however, is not the opening of the eye, but the perceiving, once the eye is open, of the ray of light set before it. But in truth the swiftness of that body differs from the twinkling of an eye as much as the agility of the mind differs from the body. The brightness of this body, too, is as great as that of spirit; for this body is not a burden to the soul but an adornment, since no corruptible mass weighs it down, but equality with the angelic nature makes it light. Its brightness, too, surpasses the sun as much as the sun surpasses our body in brightness. For the sun is a non-perceiving body, and though it be changed, it will never be given life; but that body will be perceiving, living, and intellectual. Therefore, as much as intellectual spirit differs from non-perceiving air, so much does the surpassing brightness of that body differ from the brightness of the sun.

CHAPTER XLVI. On the common and the particular glory of the saints. Here no small question arises. For since the Lord says, The just will shine like the sun (Matt. 13:43); and the Apostle, There is one brightness of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars. Star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor. 15:41): the Apostle seems to think contrary to the Lord, namely that, whereas the one asserts that they will shine like the sun, the other maintains that some will shine like various stars, others like the moon, others like the sun. But it must be understood that the Lord expressed the glory of the saints in general, while the Apostle distinguished the glory of each individual according to merits. So the last in the kingdom of heaven will shine like the sun, which will then be seven times brighter than now (Isa. 30:26). And in this brightness each differs from another according to merits as much as star differs from star in brightness. Others, again, surpass these, in the glory of differing brightness, as the morning star surpasses the Pleiades, the moon the morning star, and the sun the moon in brightness. But the body of Christ exceeds us all in brightness as much as the Creator transcends the creature; hence he is also written to sit at the right hand of God the Father (Col. 3:1), because he is believed to shine in the glory of the divine majesty. Therefore such a vision and such a glory is called the kingdom of heaven, because only the heavens, that is, the just, enjoy this vision; their reward is the highest good, in which they have full joy from the fullness of all goods.

CHAPTER XLVII. That the saints delight not in perceptible things but in the highest good. The heaven of heavens. The chain of virtues. It is concluded, therefore, that the saints do not delight in perceptible things, but glory in being in the highest good, and in enjoying the highest good by seeing it in every creature and outside every creature. For if they received anything less than the highest good as a reward, they would still desire more; and it would follow that they would not have full joy. But since it is established that they have full joy, it necessarily follows that they have God, the highest good, and abound from his abundance in the fullness of all goods. When, however, the heaven of heavens is read of, God himself is understood; because the heavens, or the just, are hidden in the secret of his face from the disturbance of men (Ps. 30:21). Hence it is written, Having treasure in heaven (Matt. 19:21), that is, in God. To this highest good the just are drawn by a certain chain, which is linked together from the virtues in this way. First, faith encircles the soul like a ring; to faith hope is attached; hope is held by love; love is fulfilled by action; action is drawn by intention toward the highest good; the intention of good is closed by perseverance; to perseverance God, the source of all goods, will be given. Therefore whoever, drawn by this chain and climbing this tower, reaches its summit will rejoice not only to know the true life, but also to live blessedly in it for ever; because in it he will be a sharer in this glory.
DISCIPLE. May God make you a sharer in true life and in all who live blessedly, and may he lead us all to the highest good. Amen.
